By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=draft}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=draft}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Special platforms and jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Region|ja|吉備国|12=draft}} incorporated {{ill|special platforms and jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|lt=Special platforms and jars|12=draft}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-shaped stone coffins were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=draft}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|ja|前方後円墳体制|12=draft}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari Site|ja|吉野ヶ里遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|ja|佐賀県|12=draft}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Itoshima City|ja|糸島市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県|12=draft}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Site|ja|平原遺跡|12=draft}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|ja|大型内行花文鏡|Large flower mirror=Large flower mirror|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|12=draft}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県|12=draft}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|ja|楯築遺跡|1=Tatetsuki Site|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|12=draft}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|ja|広島県|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} to northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} developed in the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=draft}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=draft}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Kofun Group|ja|西谷墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Izumo City|ja|出雲市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|ja|島根県|12=draft}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yasugi City|ja|安来市|12=draft}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=draft}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|ja|丹後国|12=draft}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|ja|赤坂今井墳墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府|12=draft}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海|12=draft}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|ja|ホケノ山古墳|12=draft}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped Kofuns|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=draft}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku Region|ja|北陸地方|12=draft}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=draft}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代|12=draft}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.

In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|ja|前方後円墳体制|12=draft}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari Site|ja|吉野ヶ里遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|ja|佐賀県|12=draft}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Itoshima City|ja|糸島市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県|12=draft}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Site|ja|平原遺跡|12=draft}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|ja|大型内行花文鏡|Large flower mirror=Large flower mirror|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|12=draft}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県|12=draft}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|ja|楯築遺跡|1=Tatetsuki Site|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|12=draft}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|ja|広島県|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} to northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} developed in the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=draft}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=draft}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Kofun Group|ja|西谷墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Izumo City|ja|出雲市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|ja|島根県|12=draft}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yasugi City|ja|安来市|12=draft}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=draft}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|ja|丹後国|12=draft}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|ja|赤坂今井墳墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府|12=draft}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海|12=draft}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|ja|ホケノ山古墳|12=draft}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped Kofuns|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=draft}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku Region|ja|北陸地方|12=draft}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

revision.text:
'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=draft}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代|12=draft}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=draft}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=draft}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=draft}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=draft}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Special platforms and jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Region|ja|吉備国|12=draft}} incorporated {{ill|special platforms and jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Special platforms and jars|lt=Special platforms and jars|12=draft}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-shaped stone coffins were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=draft}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.

The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yasugi City|ja|安来市|12=draft}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=draft}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.

One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|ja|赤坂今井墳墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府|12=draft}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海|12=draft}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|ja|ホケノ山古墳|12=draft}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped Kofuns|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=draft}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku Region|ja|北陸地方|12=draft}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

revision.text:
'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=draft}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代|12=draft}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=draft}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=draft}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=draft}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=draft}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Special platforms and jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Region|ja|吉備国|12=draft}} incorporated {{ill|special platforms and jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Special platforms and jars|1=Special platforms and jars|lt=Special platforms and jars|12=draft}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-shaped stone coffins were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=draft}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|ja|前方後円墳体制|12=draft}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari Site|ja|吉野ヶ里遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|ja|佐賀県|12=draft}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Itoshima City|ja|糸島市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県|12=draft}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Site|ja|平原遺跡|12=draft}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|ja|大型内行花文鏡|Large flower mirror=Large flower mirror|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|12=draft}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県|12=draft}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|ja|楯築遺跡|1=Tatetsuki Site|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|12=draft}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|ja|広島県|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} to northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} developed in the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=draft}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=draft}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Kofun Group|ja|西谷墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Izumo City|ja|出雲市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|ja|島根県|12=draft}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yasugi City|ja|安来市|12=draft}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=draft}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|ja|丹後国|12=draft}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|ja|赤坂今井墳墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府|12=draft}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海|12=draft}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|ja|ホケノ山古墳|12=draft}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped Kofuns|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=draft}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku Region|ja|北陸地方|12=draft}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=draft}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代|12=draft}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=draft}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=draft}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=draft}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=draft}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Special platforms and jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Region|ja|吉備国|12=draft}} incorporated {{ill|special platforms and jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Special platforms and jars|1=Special platforms and jars|lt=Special platforms and jars|12=draft}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-shaped stone coffins were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=draft}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|ja|前方後円墳体制|12=draft}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari Site|ja|吉野ヶ里遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|ja|佐賀県|12=draft}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Itoshima City|ja|糸島市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県|12=draft}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Site|ja|平原遺跡|12=draft}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|ja|大型内行花文鏡|Large flower mirror=Large flower mirror|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|12=draft}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県|12=draft}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|ja|楯築遺跡|1=Tatetsuki Site|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|12=draft}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|ja|広島県|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} to northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} developed in the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=draft}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=draft}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Kofun Group|ja|西谷墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Izumo City|ja|出雲市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|ja|島根県|12=draft}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yasugi City|ja|安来市|12=draft}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=draft}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|ja|丹後国|12=draft}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|ja|赤坂今井墳墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府|12=draft}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海|12=draft}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|ja|ホケノ山古墳|12=draft}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped Kofuns|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=draft}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku Region|ja|北陸地方|12=draft}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=draft}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代|12=draft}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=draft}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=draft}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=draft}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=draft}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=draft}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Special platforms and jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Region|ja|吉備国|12=draft}} incorporated {{ill|special platforms and jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Special platforms and jars|1=Special platforms and jars|lt=Special platforms and jars|12=draft}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-shaped stone coffins were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=draft}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|ja|前方後円墳体制|12=draft}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari Site|ja|吉野ヶ里遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|ja|佐賀県|12=draft}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=draft}} in {{ill|Itoshima City|ja|糸島市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県|12=draft}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Site|ja|平原遺跡|12=draft}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|ja|大型内行花文鏡|Large flower mirror=Large flower mirror|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|12=draft}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Hyogo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県|12=draft}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|ja|楯築遺跡|1=Tatetsuki Site|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kurashiki City|ja|倉敷市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県|12=draft}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|ja|広島県|12=draft}} through the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} to northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=draft}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=draft}} developed in the {{ill|Chugoku Mountains|ja|中国山地|12=draft}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=draft}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=draft}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=draft}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Kofun Group|ja|西谷墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Izumo City|ja|出雲市|12=draft}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|ja|島根県|12=draft}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=draft}} in {{ill|Yasugi City|ja|安来市|12=draft}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=draft}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kinki Region|ja|近畿地方|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|ja|丹後国|12=draft}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|ja|赤坂今井墳墓|12=draft}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府|12=draft}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|ja|日本海|12=draft}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|ja|ホケノ山古墳|12=draft}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県|12=draft}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped Kofuns|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=draft}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku Region|ja|北陸地方|12=draft}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

revision.text:
'''弥生墳丘墓'''（やよいふんきゅうぼ）は、日本の[[弥生時代]]の[[墳丘墓]]（墳丘をもつ[[墓]]）を指す{{efn|後述の{{harv|和田|2003}}の定義に従う。}}。[[弥生時代の墓制]]の一つ。
弥生墳丘墓がもつ諸要素の継承と飛躍をもって[[古墳時代]]の[[古墳]]が誕生したと考えられる<ref>{{harv|近藤|1983}}、{{harv|近藤|1986}}ほか</ref>。
== 概要 == 弥生時代前期に、墓室上に盛り土をした墳丘墓が築造されるようになり、円丘や方丘が作られた。
弥生時代後期に、墳丘（[[盛土]]）を形成した後、墓穴を掘削する形態が現れ、また墳丘の大型化と突出部の形成が現れた。これらは古墳時代の古墳へ引き継がれたと考えられている。 <!--これら弥生墳丘墓の中には[[前方後円墳]]の前方部のような突出部が付く墳丘墓も出てくる。つまりこの頃になって墳丘の大型化と突出部の形成が始まる。-->
=== 定義 === 弥生墳丘墓という概念は[[1977年]]に[[近藤義郎]]が提唱したこと{{sfn|近藤|1977}}に始まる。近藤は「おもに溝によって」墓域を区画する[[周溝墓]]、「おもに周囲の削り出しによって」墓域を区画する[[台状墓]]に対し、「おもに盛土によって墓域を画し形成しようとしているらしい一群」を区別するため墳丘墓あるいは弥生墳丘墓と呼んだ{{sfn|近藤|1977|p=1}}{{efn|近藤は三者を厳密に分けることが困難であるとしており{{sfn|近藤|1977|pp=1-2}}、この時点ではあくまで暫定的な用語であった。}}。
この定義に対し、[[都出比呂志]]は大阪府[[瓜生堂遺跡]]などの例をもとに「盛土の程度という指標のみでは[[方形周溝墓]]、方形台状墓、墳丘墓の三者を質的には区別しがたい」{{sfn|都出|1979|p=19}}とし、「古墳をも含めた、墳丘を有する墓」{{sfn|都出|1986|p=222}}の総称として「墳丘墓」という用語を設け、これを細分する試みを提唱した{{sfn|都出|1979}}{{sfn|都出|1986}}{{efn|都出は、とくに古墳時代の「低墳丘古墳」について超時代的に理解して「低墳丘墓」に一括するのが妥当であるとする{{harv|都出|1986|p=224}}。同一の系譜上に位置するこれらの「低墳丘墓」が古墳時代に属するとき「『古墳』なる特殊呼称をも有することになる」{{harv|都出|1986|p=224}}というように、弥生墳丘墓と古墳との差異を時代の差においていた。ただしこの論文上で「弥生墳丘墓」の呼称は現れない。}}。
都出の定義は[[2003年]]の時点で「学会でも一定の支持を得つつある」{{sfn|和田|2003|p=3}}一方で、「個々の研究者が用いる用語の概念にはいまだ少なからず混乱が見られる」{{sfn|和田|2003|p=4}}状況にあったため、[[和田晴吾]]が用語の再整理を試みている。そこでは「墳丘を持つ墓」を「墳丘墓」と総称した上で、[[弥生時代]]のものについて「'''弥生墳丘墓'''」と呼称するとしている{{sfn|和田|2003|p=4}}。その上で、墳形、墳丘の築造法、立地、周溝墓と台状墓の複合・使い分け、墓坑の構築技法の観点から細分した{{sfn|和田|2003}}。
=== 墳形 === 基本型式として方形周溝墓、円形周溝墓、方形台状墓、円形台状墓が挙げられる{{sfn|和田|2003|pp=7-8}}。周溝墓と台状墓には使い分けが見られる例もある{{sfn|和田|2003|p=9}}。それぞれの基本型式の地域的な変容として、[[方形貼石墓]]（方形貼石台状墓・方形貼石周溝墓）や[[四隅突出型墳丘墓]]（四隅突出型方形台状墓・四隅突出型方形周溝墓）などがある{{sfn|和田|2003|pp=8-10}}。
'''方形周溝墓'''は四周{{efn|一部の場合もある。}}に溝を掘って盛土をする形態の墳墓で、弥生墳丘墓としてはもっとも多く発見されている。おもに集落近くの平地に築造される。弥生時代前期前葉には北部九州や近畿で出現しており、近畿を中心にして各地に拡散する{{sfn|和田|2003|p=7}}。
'''円形周溝墓'''は墳丘の造り方や埋葬施設などは方形周溝墓に類似するが、円形プランの墳丘墓である。弥生時代前期中葉に瀬戸内に出現して以降、各地に広がっていく{{sfn|和田|2003|p=7}}。
'''方形台状墓'''は地山を削り出して成形する形態の墳墓である。おもに丘陵上に築造される。弥生時代前期末から中期初頭ごろに現れ、中国地方や日本海沿岸に多く所在する{{sfn|和田|2003|pp=7-8}}{{efn|この分布は方形周溝墓とは総体的な地域差を示す{{sfn|和田|2003|p=7}}。}}。
'''円形台状墓'''は数が少なく、弥生時代後期後半の瀬戸内などに認められる{{sfn|和田|2003|p=8}}。
=== 特殊器台・特殊壺 === {{main|特殊器台・特殊壺}} 弥生時代後期に[[吉備国|吉備地域]]において、弥生墳丘墓での埋葬祭祀に[[特殊器台・特殊壺]]と呼ばれる土器が使用された{{sfn|近藤|春成|1967}}。これらの土器は吉備地域を中心としながら、特定の時期の[[出雲国|山陰地域西部]]や[[讃岐国|瀬戸内海沿岸東部地域]]、[[畿内|近畿中部]]にも分布している{{sfn|宇垣|2016|pp=46-48}}。
=== 棺と槨 === 弥生墳丘墓の棺は短く、内法で約2メートルの組合せ箱形木棺が盛行する。北部九州などでは組合せ箱式石棺が使われる。棺を納める槨も棺に応じた長さで、木槨・石槨がある。最終的には石槨が使われ、前方後円墳の石槨に繋がる。楯築弥生墳丘墓の木槨は長さ約3.5メートル、木棺の長さ約2メートルで、木槨は二重底になっている。
最古式の前方後円墳（[[出現期古墳]]）が出現する頃には、槨が石槨になり、木蓋は石蓋に変わり、棺も[[割竹形木棺|割竹形]]・箱形と格差が現れる。
=== 副葬品 === 種類が貧弱で、やりがんな1本、あるいはガラス小玉2、3個、鉄剣1本しか埋葬されていない場合もあり、何も副葬されない埋葬が多い。最大の楯築弥生墳丘墓でも、剣1本、首飾り2連、小玉小管玉群一括にすぎなかった。
ところで、北部九州の弥生時代前期末、中期の副葬品は多くの韓製[[銅剣]]、[[銅矛]]、[[銅戈]]などの[[青銅器]]、大陸製の青銅器や璧（へき）、その他玉類などが豊かであった。しかし、後期後葉には、副葬の慣習が変化したのか副葬品が吉備や[[出雲国|出雲]]と同じく貧弱になった。その理由について、今日よく分かっていない。
しかし、古墳時代に入ると、副葬品の量・質・ともに豊かになり、身分の差を表現するようになったと考えられている。
== 展開 == 方形・円形周溝墓は、墓の四周に溝を掘り主に平地に築かれ、墓の周囲の地山を削り出す台状墓は主に丘陵上に築かれた。その他の墳丘墓も三形式の変容型として地域型{{efn|貼石方形台状墓、四隅突出型方形台状墓など。}}、階層型{{efn|前方状方形墳丘墓や前方後円墳丘墓など。}}、複合型{{efn|貼石方形周溝墓、四隅突出型方形周溝墓、丘陵上の方形周溝墓など。}}などに区分することができる。そして、特徴は、首長墓の出現と展開であり、地方色の顕著な現れである。それは、各地における首長層の成長と、地域的・地方的段階での政治的結びつき（首長連合）の形成過程であった。
弥生時代前期から中期においては、西日本の各地に各種の墳丘墓が拡がるが、墳丘規模に大きな格差のない段階である。方形周溝墓は畿内から近江、伊勢湾沿岸の東海西部に定着し、西は播磨から東は関東・北陸の西部まで拡散する。円形周溝墓は瀬戸内中部に出現し、播磨に拡がり、その後は徐々に東に拡がる。方形台状墓は近畿北部・北陸・東海の一部に出現する。
弥生時代中期後葉から後期前半にかけては、墳丘規模に格差が広がり、墳長20メートル以上の大型墓が出現する。それらは首長・地域有力者の墓と推定される。また、中国地方北部や山陰、近畿北部に地域的特色を有する墳丘墓が築造されだした。この時期から次の時期にかけて[[石器]]から[[鉄器]]使用が本格化し始める。[[朝鮮半島]]南部で産出する鉄素材の流通機構の移行・再編が地方レベルまでおよび、首長層の政治的連合や同盟が、これまで以上に推進したと考えられる。
弥生時代後期後半から終末期にかけては、一部の墳丘墓で突出部が発達し、首長墓専用の墳形が成立する。一方では他の墳丘墓が小型化し、さらに最下層墓が密集型[[土坑墓]]となっていく。共同体の階層分化が急速に進行し、共同体村落の[[環濠集落]]が解体の道をたどる。各地には核となる墳丘墓が現れて地域が連合し、さらに地方が連合し、それらの段階で共通の墳丘墓型式を採用することにより他地方との区別を明確にしていったと推定する{{sfn|和田|2004}}。
=== 弥生墳丘墓から前方後円墳へ === 墳丘墓の突出部が一見前方部の原形のようになってくるのは、[[中国山地]]では弥生中期後葉から、山陰では後期後葉から、北陸では少し遅れ、吉備では後期後葉からである。
以上のように、弥生時代後期後葉には、弥生墳丘墓が地域ごとに独自な形式で成立するとともに、地域ごとの祭祀的世界や政治的勢力が形成されていたと考えられる。
古墳時代に入ると前方後円墳が巨大化し、突出部は、前方部に整えられていく。さらに、墳丘の形と規模において格差が明瞭に現れて、前方後円墳・前方後方墳・円形・方形といった'''[[前方後円墳体制]]'''を形成する{{sfn|渡辺|2007}}。
== 各地の墳丘墓 == === 北部九州 === [[佐賀県]][[吉野ヶ里遺跡]]の墳丘墓は、南北約46メートル、東西約27メートルで長方形に近く、高さ4.5メートル以上あったと推定されている。墓壙を頂上から掘って14基以上の甕棺を埋置している。甕棺は弥生時代中期のもので、この時期になぜ大型墳丘墓が出現したのかについてはまだ明確に分かっていない。
中期後半には、王墓とされる墳丘墓が出現する。福岡県[[糸島市]][[三雲南小路遺跡]]は溝で囲まれた一辺30メートル以上の墳丘で王墓と推定され、2基の甕棺から57枚の以上の中国鏡が出土している。
後期には同じ糸島市の[[平原遺跡|平原1号墓]]で[[大型内行花文鏡]]を含む40面の[[銅鏡]]が副葬された。
=== 瀬戸内 === [[兵庫県]]揖保川町養久山5号弥生墳丘墓は、墳長約20メートル、前後に突出部が造られており、高さ約1.5から2メートルと推測される。
岡山県倉敷市の[[楯築遺跡|楯築弥生墳丘墓]]は大型で、突出部を含めた墳丘の長さが80メートル、円丘の高さは約4.5メートルもある。突出部には列石が2列に巡らされていた。
=== 山陰 === [[広島県]]北部の[[中国山地]]から近畿地方北部にかけて、弥生時代中期から後期前半に[[方形貼石墓]]が造られるようになる{{sfn|肥後|2010}}。
弥生時代中期後葉には、[[中国山地]]と[[出雲平野]]に貼石方形墓の発展した[[四隅突出型墳丘墓|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓]]が生まれ、以後[[中国山地]]と[[鳥取平野]]から[[出雲平野]]および[[隠岐国|隠岐]]にわたる山陰地域で盛行する。島根県[[出雲市]][[西谷墳墓群]]では6基の四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓が造られ、そのなかには東西の辺約40メートル、南北の辺約30メートル、高さ約4.5メートルという大きなもの（3号墓）もある。島根県[[安来市]]は日本最大の四隅突出墳丘墓の集中地帯（[[荒島墳墓群]]{{efn|荒島地域の弥生時代から古墳時代にかけての墳墓群の総称だが、このうち[[仲仙寺古墳群|仲仙寺墳墓群]]・安養寺墳墓群・塩津山墳墓群・下山墳墓群で四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓が築造されている。}}）であり、古墳時代までほぼ継続的に様々な形の首長墓が造られた。
=== 近畿北部 === 近畿地方北部の[[丹後国|丹後]]地域に、豪華な副葬品をもつ大形の墳丘墓が弥生時代終末期に出現している。それは[[京都府]][[赤坂今井墳墓]]で、37×35メートル、高さ4.2メートルほどの方形墳丘墓である。墳頂中央には巨大な墓壙が発見されているが、棺などはまだである。出土土器から3世紀初めで、この地域の政治的集団の王の墓であろうと推定されている。丹後は[[日本海]]沿岸にありながら上述の山陰・北陸とは異なり、四隅突出型墳丘墓の分布がみられない地域である。
=== 近畿中央部 === 奈良県の[[ホケノ山古墳]]は前方後円形の墳丘で、弥生墳丘墓であるとする見方と古墳時代のものとする見方が出されている{{efn|本古墳について、寺沢薫は、箸墓古墳よりも先に築造された6基の「[[纒向型前方後円墳]]」の中にふくめている{{sfn|寺沢|1988}}。}}。
=== 北陸 === 弥生時代後期に、北陸地方でも四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓が築造される{{sfn|古川|1993}}。
=== 東海 === {{節stub}}
