revision.text:
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]]
'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period funerary practices|13=User:Immanuelle/Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|qq=}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kondō Yoshio|1=Yoshirō Kondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638900}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated graves|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/terraced tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsunode Hiroshi|1=Tsude Hiroshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11643486}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wada Harugo|1=Seigo Wada|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418030}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square mounds|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/protruded-corner square mounds|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|qq=}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Region|1=Kingdom of Kibi}} incorporated {{ill|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|lt=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|qq=}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-type Sarcophaguss were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/proto-kofun|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Kofun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari site|en|Yoshinogari site|WD=Q1049645|lt=Yoshinogari Site|1=Yoshinogari site}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|en|Saga Prefecture|WD=Q160420|lt=Saga Prefecture|1=Saga Prefecture}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikumo Nanokoji Site|qq=}} in {{ill|Itoshima, Fukuoka|en|Itoshima, Fukuoka|WD=Q1011145|lt=Itoshima City|1=Itoshima}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Ruins|ja|平原遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirabaru Site|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|en|Large flower mirror|WD=Q11433747|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|1=Large flower mirror}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|en|Tatetsuki Site|WD=Q11541408|lt=Tatetsuki Site|1=Tatetsuki Site}} in {{ill|Kurashiki|en|Kurashiki|WD=Q467487|lt=Kurashiki City|1=Kurashiki}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}} through the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} to northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四隅突出型墳丘墓}} developed in the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumo Plain|1=Izumo Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11395890}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tottori Plain|1=Tottori Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11674508}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oki Islands|1=Oki Province|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11659029}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|en|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|WD=Q11629514|lt=Nishidani Kofun Group|1=Nishidani Kofun cluster}} in {{ill|Izumo, Shimane|en|Izumo, Shimane|WD=Q825166|lt=Izumo City|1=Izumo, Shimane}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Arashima Kofun Cluster|qq=}} in {{ill|Yasugi, Shimane|en|Yasugi, Shimane|WD=Q851114|lt=Yasugi City|1=Yasugi, Shimane}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|en|Akasakaimai Tumuli|WD=Q11635401|lt=Akasakaimai Tumuli|1=Akasakaimai Tumuli}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan|1=Sea of Japan}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|en|Hokenoyama Kofun|WD=Q11337664|lt=Hokenoyama Kofun|1=Hokenoyama Kofun}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|qq=}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku Region|1=Hokuriku region}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.
=== Tokai === {{Section stub}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]]
'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period funerary practices|13=User:Immanuelle/Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|qq=}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kondō Yoshio|1=Yoshirō Kondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638900}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated graves|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/terraced tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsunode Hiroshi|1=Tsude Hiroshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11643486}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wada Harugo|1=Seigo Wada|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418030}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square mounds|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/protruded-corner square mounds|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|qq=}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Region|1=Kingdom of Kibi}} incorporated {{ill|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|lt=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|qq=}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-type Sarcophaguss were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/proto-kofun|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Kofun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari site|en|Yoshinogari site|WD=Q1049645|lt=Yoshinogari Site|1=Yoshinogari site}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|en|Saga Prefecture|WD=Q160420|lt=Saga Prefecture|1=Saga Prefecture}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikumo Nanokoji Site|qq=}} in {{ill|Itoshima, Fukuoka|en|Itoshima, Fukuoka|WD=Q1011145|lt=Itoshima City|1=Itoshima}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Ruins|ja|平原遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirabaru Site|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|en|Large flower mirror|WD=Q11433747|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|1=Large flower mirror}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|en|Tatetsuki Site|WD=Q11541408|lt=Tatetsuki Site|1=Tatetsuki Site}} in {{ill|Kurashiki|en|Kurashiki|WD=Q467487|lt=Kurashiki City|1=Kurashiki}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}} through the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} to northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四隅突出型墳丘墓}} developed in the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumo Plain|1=Izumo Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11395890}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tottori Plain|1=Tottori Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11674508}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oki Islands|1=Oki Province|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11659029}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|en|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|WD=Q11629514|lt=Nishidani Kofun Group|1=Nishidani Kofun cluster}} in {{ill|Izumo, Shimane|en|Izumo, Shimane|WD=Q825166|lt=Izumo City|1=Izumo, Shimane}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Arashima Kofun Cluster|qq=}} in {{ill|Yasugi, Shimane|en|Yasugi, Shimane|WD=Q851114|lt=Yasugi City|1=Yasugi, Shimane}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|en|Akasakaimai Tumuli|WD=Q11635401|lt=Akasakaimai Tumuli|1=Akasakaimai Tumuli}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan|1=Sea of Japan}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|en|Hokenoyama Kofun|WD=Q11337664|lt=Hokenoyama Kofun|1=Hokenoyama Kofun}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|qq=}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku Region|1=Hokuriku region}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]]
'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period funerary practices|13=User:Immanuelle/Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|qq=}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kondō Yoshio|1=Yoshirō Kondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638900}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated graves|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/terraced tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsunode Hiroshi|1=Tsude Hiroshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11643486}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wada Harugo|1=Seigo Wada|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418030}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square mounds|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/protruded-corner square mounds|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|qq=}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Region|1=Kingdom of Kibi}} incorporated {{ill|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|lt=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|qq=}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-type Sarcophaguss were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/proto-kofun|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Kofun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari site|en|Yoshinogari site|WD=Q1049645|lt=Yoshinogari Site|1=Yoshinogari site}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|en|Saga Prefecture|WD=Q160420|lt=Saga Prefecture|1=Saga Prefecture}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikumo Nanokoji Site|qq=}} in {{ill|Itoshima, Fukuoka|en|Itoshima, Fukuoka|WD=Q1011145|lt=Itoshima City|1=Itoshima}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Ruins|ja|平原遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirabaru Site|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|en|Large flower mirror|WD=Q11433747|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|1=Large flower mirror}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|en|Tatetsuki Site|WD=Q11541408|lt=Tatetsuki Site|1=Tatetsuki Site}} in {{ill|Kurashiki|en|Kurashiki|WD=Q467487|lt=Kurashiki City|1=Kurashiki}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}} through the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} to northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四隅突出型墳丘墓}} developed in the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumo Plain|1=Izumo Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11395890}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tottori Plain|1=Tottori Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11674508}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oki Islands|1=Oki Province|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11659029}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|en|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|WD=Q11629514|lt=Nishidani Kofun Group|1=Nishidani Kofun cluster}} in {{ill|Izumo, Shimane|en|Izumo, Shimane|WD=Q825166|lt=Izumo City|1=Izumo, Shimane}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Arashima Kofun Cluster|qq=}} in {{ill|Yasugi, Shimane|en|Yasugi, Shimane|WD=Q851114|lt=Yasugi City|1=Yasugi, Shimane}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|en|Akasakaimai Tumuli|WD=Q11635401|lt=Akasakaimai Tumuli|1=Akasakaimai Tumuli}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan|1=Sea of Japan}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|en|Hokenoyama Kofun|WD=Q11337664|lt=Hokenoyama Kofun|1=Hokenoyama Kofun}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|qq=}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku Region|1=Hokuriku region}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:弥生墳丘墓]][[ko:야요이분구묘]]
'''Yayoi Kofuns''' (弥生墳丘墓) refer to Kofuns with raised earthen structures from the {{ill|Yayoi period|en|Yayoi period|WD=Q207858|lt=Yayoi period|1=Yayoi period}} of Japan{{efn|Defined as per {{harv|Wada|2003}} mentioned below.}}. These represent one of the {{ill|Yayoi period funerary practices|ja|弥生時代の墓制|1=Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yayoi period funerary practices|13=User:Immanuelle/Funerary practices of the Yayoi period|qq=}}.
The evolution and development of elements present in Yayoi Kofuns are believed to have led to the emergence of the {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}<ref>{{harv|Kondō|1983}}, {{harv|Kondō|1986}}, among others</ref>.
== Overview == During the early Yayoi period, Kofuns with soil heaped over burial chambers began to be constructed, forming circular and square mounds.
In the late Yayoi period, a new form emerged where the mound (heaped soil) was constructed first, followed by the excavation of the burial pit. This period also saw the enlargement of Kofuns and the formation of protruding sections, which are thought to have been carried over into the kofun (ancient tomb) of the Kofun period.
=== Definition === The concept of Yayoi Kofuns was first proposed by {{ill|Kondō Yoshio|ja|近藤義郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kondō Yoshio|1=Yoshirō Kondō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638900}} in 1977{{sfn|Kondō|1977}}. Kondō defined Yayoi Kofuns as "a group of tombs that appear to delineate and form the burial area primarily through heaped soil," distinguishing them from {{ill|moated graves|ja|周溝墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/moated graves|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily through trenches" and {{ill|terraced tombs|ja|台状墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/terraced tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} that define burial areas "primarily by surrounding earth-cut areas"{{sfn|Kondō|1977|p=1}}{{efn|Kondō noted that it was difficult to strictly separate these three types and regarded the terms as provisional at the time{{sfn|Kondō|1977|pp=1-2}}.}}.
Building on Kondō's definition, {{ill|Tsunode Hiroshi|ja|都出比呂志|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsunode Hiroshi|1=Tsude Hiroshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11643486}} proposed the term "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds," including kofun, and suggested classifying them into more specific categories{{sfn|Tsunode|1979}}{{sfn|Tsunode|1986}}{{efn|Tsunode argued that the low-mounded kofun of the Kofun period should be understood as "low-mounded tombs" within the same lineage as Yayoi Kofuns, differing primarily in historical period{{sfn|Tsunode|1986|p=224}}.}}.
By 2003, Tsunode's broader definition had gained significant academic support{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=3}}, though some confusion persisted in terminology among researchers{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. {{ill|Wada Harugo|ja|和田晴吾|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wada Harugo|1=Seigo Wada|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418030}} attempted to reorganize the terms, using "Kofuns" as a general term for "tombs with mounds" and designating those from the Yayoi period specifically as "Yayoi Kofuns"{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=4}}. He further classified them by mound shape, construction methods, location, and burial techniques{{sfn|Wada|2003}}.
=== Mound Shapes === The basic types include square moated mounds, circular moated mounds, square terraced mounds, and circular terraced mounds{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}. Variations include {{ill|stone-lined square mounds|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square mounds|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|protruded-corner square mounds|ja|四隅突出型墳丘墓|1=X-shaped Burial Mound|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/protruded-corner square mounds|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|qq=}}{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=8-10}}.
'''Square moated mounds''' are Kofuns surrounded by trenches and covered with heaped soil, primarily located near settlements in plains. They first appeared in the early Yayoi period in northern Kyushu and the Kinki region, spreading to other areas{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Circular moated mounds''' are similar to square moated mounds but with circular layouts. They appeared in the mid-early Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area and later spread{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=7}}.
'''Square terraced mounds''' are mounds shaped by cutting and leveling natural ground, primarily constructed on hills. They appeared from the late early Yayoi period to the early middle Yayoi period, mainly in the Chugoku region and along the Sea of Japan coast{{sfn|Wada|2003|pp=7-8}}.
'''Circular terraced mounds''' are rare and found in the late Yayoi period in the Seto Inland Sea area{{sfn|Wada|2003|p=8}}.
=== Special Platforms and Vessels === {{main|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars}} In the late Yayoi period, burial rituals in the {{ill|Kibi Province|en|Kibi Province|WD=Q1155128|lt=Kibi Region|1=Kingdom of Kibi}} incorporated {{ill|Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|ja|特殊器台・特殊壺|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|1=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|lt=Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|13=User:Immanuelle/Ceremonial vessel stands or jars|qq=}}. These artifacts are centered in the Kibi region but also distributed in the western San’in region, eastern Seto Inland Sea, and central Kinki{{sfn|Kondō|Harunari|1967}}{{sfn|Ugaki|2016|pp=46-48}}.
=== Coffins and Chambers === Yayoi Kofuns typically used short composite box-shaped wooden coffins, about 2 meters long internally. In northern Kyushu, composite box-type Sarcophaguss were also common. Chambers matched the coffin sizes and included wooden and stone types. Later, stone chambers became predominant, connecting to the stone chambers of early kofun.
By the time the earliest kofun ({{ill|proto-kofun|ja|出現期古墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/proto-kofun|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) appeared, chambers transitioned to stone, lids became stone, and coffins varied in form, showing social stratification.
=== Grave Goods === Yayoi burial goods were often sparse, sometimes limited to a single tool or a few glass beads. In rare cases, items such as swords and necklaces were found, but lavish burials were uncommon.
In contrast, burials in northern Kyushu during the mid-Yayoi period included imported bronze weapons and jade ornaments. However, in the late Yayoi period, grave goods became sparse in Kyushu, Kibi, and Izumo. The reasons for this decline remain unclear. By the Kofun period, burial practices shifted to emphasize social hierarchy through elaborate grave goods. == Development == Square and circular moated tombs were constructed with trenches dug on all four sides, primarily on flatlands. In contrast, terraced tombs, which involved cutting and leveling the natural ground surrounding the burial site, were mainly built on hills. Other Kofuns can be categorized as regional variants{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square terraced tombs and protruded-corner square terraced tombs.}}, hierarchical types{{efn|Examples include rectangular tombs with a front section and mound tombs with keyhole-shaped mounds.}}, and composite types{{efn|Examples include stone-lined square moated tombs, protruded-corner square moated tombs, and square moated tombs built on hills.}}. A notable feature is the emergence and development of chieftain tombs, which prominently reflect regional characteristics. These tombs illustrate the growth of the chieftain class in various regions and the formation of regional and local political alliances (chieftain unions).
During the early to middle Yayoi period, various types of Kofuns spread across western Japan, with minimal disparity in mound size. Square moated tombs became established from Kinki to Omi and the western part of Ise Bay in Tokai, spreading westward to Harima and eastward to western Kanto and Hokuriku. Circular moated tombs appeared in central Seto Inland Sea and expanded to Harima, gradually spreading further east. Square terraced tombs emerged in northern Kinki, Hokuriku, and parts of Tokai.
From the late middle Yayoi period to the early late Yayoi period, disparities in mound sizes increased, and large tombs exceeding 20 meters in length appeared. These are presumed to be the tombs of chieftains and regional elites. During this time, regional Kofun styles with distinct characteristics began to be constructed in northern Chugoku, San'in, and northern Kinki. Additionally, the transition to the use of iron tools and weapons from stone tools became prominent during this period. The distribution and reorganization of iron materials sourced from the southern Korean Peninsula extended to local levels, facilitating further political alliances and cooperation among chieftains.
In the late Yayoi period's latter half to its terminal phase, some Kofuns developed prominent protrusions, leading to the establishment of exclusive mound shapes for chieftain tombs. Meanwhile, other Kofuns became smaller, and lower-class graves evolved into densely packed pit graves. This period saw rapid social stratification within communities, leading to the disintegration of moated settlements. Prominent Kofuns began to serve as nuclei for regional and eventually interregional alliances. The adoption of shared Kofun styles at these levels likely distinguished these regions from others{{sfn|Wada|2004}}.
=== From Yayoi Kofuns to Keyhole-Shaped Tombs === The development of protrusions resembling the early form of front sections of keyhole-shaped mounds began in the latter half of the middle Yayoi period in the Chugoku Mountains, in the latter half of the late Yayoi period in San'in, slightly later in Hokuriku, and from the latter half of the late Yayoi period in Kibi.
Thus, by the latter half of the late Yayoi period, Yayoi Kofuns had evolved into distinct regional forms, reflecting the unique ritualistic and political landscapes of each area.
In the Kofun period, keyhole-shaped mounds grew larger, with protrusions forming refined front sections. Disparities in mound shapes and sizes became more pronounced, culminating in the formation of the '''{{ill|Kofun system|en|Kofun system|WD=Q11397224|lt=Kofun system|1=Keyhole tomb order}}''', encompassing keyhole-shaped, rectangular, circular, and square tombs{{sfn|Watanabe|2007}}. == Regional Yayoi Kofuns == === Northern Kyushu === The Kofun at the {{ill|Yoshinogari site|en|Yoshinogari site|WD=Q1049645|lt=Yoshinogari Site|1=Yoshinogari site}} in {{ill|Saga Prefecture|en|Saga Prefecture|WD=Q160420|lt=Saga Prefecture|1=Saga Prefecture}} is estimated to have been nearly rectangular, measuring approximately 46 meters north-south and 27 meters east-west, with a height of over 4.5 meters. The burial pit contained more than 14 jar burials, which date back to the middle Yayoi period. The reason for the emergence of large-scale Kofuns during this period remains unclear.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, royal tombs began to appear. The Kofun at the {{ill|Mikumo Nanokoji Site|ja|三雲南小路遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mikumo Nanokoji Site|qq=}} in {{ill|Itoshima, Fukuoka|en|Itoshima, Fukuoka|WD=Q1011145|lt=Itoshima City|1=Itoshima}}, {{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|en|Fukuoka Prefecture|WD=Q123258|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}, is a moated square tomb over 30 meters on each side, believed to be a royal tomb. Fifty-seven or more Chinese bronze mirrors were excavated from two jar burials.
In the late Yayoi period, at the {{ill|Hirabaru Ruins|ja|平原遺跡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirabaru Site|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} in the same Itoshima City, the first tomb contained 40 bronze mirrors, including a large {{ill|Large flower mirror|en|Large flower mirror|WD=Q11433747|lt=inner-patterned flower mirror|1=Large flower mirror}} as grave goods.
=== Seto Inland Sea Region === The Yayoi Kofun at {{ill|Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja|養久山5号弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yokuyama Site No. 5|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|en|Hyōgo Prefecture|WD=Q130290|lt=Hyōgo Prefecture|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}} has an estimated mound length of about 20 meters with protrusions at both ends, standing approximately 1.5 to 2 meters high.
The {{ill|Tatetsuki Site|en|Tatetsuki Site|WD=Q11541408|lt=Tatetsuki Site|1=Tatetsuki Site}} in {{ill|Kurashiki|en|Kurashiki|WD=Q467487|lt=Kurashiki City|1=Kurashiki}}, {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}, is large, measuring 80 meters in mound length (including protrusions) and about 4.5 meters in height. The protrusions are encircled by two rows of standing stones.
=== San'in Region === From the northern part of {{ill|Hiroshima Prefecture|en|Hiroshima Prefecture|WD=Q617375|lt=Hiroshima Prefecture|1=Hiroshima Prefecture}} through the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} to northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, {{ill|stone-lined square tombs|ja|方形貼石墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone-lined square tombs|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} began to be constructed during the middle Yayoi period{{sfn|Higo|2010}}.
In the latter half of the middle Yayoi period, {{ill|X-shaped Burial Mound|lt=X-shaped Burial Mounds|ja|四隅突出型弥生墳丘墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/X-shaped Burial Mound|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 四隅突出型墳丘墓}} developed in the {{ill|Chūgoku Mountains|en|Chūgoku Mountains|WD=Q857567|lt=Chugoku Mountains|1=Chūgoku Mountains}} and {{ill|Izumo Plain|ja|出雲平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izumo Plain|1=Izumo Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11395890}}, becoming prominent burial sites throughout the San'in region, including the {{ill|Tottori Plain|ja|鳥取平野|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tottori Plain|1=Tottori Plain|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11674508}} and {{ill|Oki Islands|ja|隠岐|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oki Islands|1=Oki Province|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11659029}}. At the {{ill|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|en|Nishidani Tumulus cluster|WD=Q11629514|lt=Nishidani Kofun Group|1=Nishidani Kofun cluster}} in {{ill|Izumo, Shimane|en|Izumo, Shimane|WD=Q825166|lt=Izumo City|1=Izumo, Shimane}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|WD=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}, six protruded-corner mounds were constructed. Among them, Tomb No. 3 measured approximately 40 meters east-west, 30 meters north-south, and about 4.5 meters in height. The {{ill|Arashima Kofun Cluster|ja|荒島墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Arashima Kofun Cluster|qq=}} in {{ill|Yasugi, Shimane|en|Yasugi, Shimane|WD=Q851114|lt=Yasugi City|1=Yasugi, Shimane}} is the largest concentration of protruded-corner mounds in Japan and saw continuous construction of various chieftain tombs through the Kofun period{{efn|This cluster includes the {{ill|Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja|仲仙寺墳墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakasenji Kofun Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, Anyoji Kofun Group, Shiozuyama Kofun Group, and Shimoyama Kofun Group.}}.
=== Northern Kinki === In the northern {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kinki Region|1=Kansai region}}, the {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} area saw the emergence of large Kofuns with luxurious grave goods during the terminal Yayoi period. One such example is the {{ill|Akasakaimai Tumuli|en|Akasakaimai Tumuli|WD=Q11635401|lt=Akasakaimai Tumuli|1=Akasakaimai Tumuli}} in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, measuring 37 by 35 meters and about 4.2 meters in height. A large burial pit was discovered at its summit, but no coffin has been unearthed. Based on excavated pottery, the mound dates to the early 3rd century and is believed to be the tomb of a political leader in the region. Despite its location along the {{ill|Sea of Japan|en|Sea of Japan|WD=Q27092|lt=Sea of Japan|1=Sea of Japan}}, the Tango area lacks evidence of protruded-corner mounds found in other regions like San'in and Hokuriku.
=== Central Kinki === The {{ill|Hokenoyama Kofun|en|Hokenoyama Kofun|WD=Q11337664|lt=Hokenoyama Kofun|1=Hokenoyama Kofun}} in {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} is a Kofun with a keyhole-shaped plan. It is debated whether it represents a Yayoi Kofun or belongs to the Kofun period{{efn|Kaoru Terasawa includes this mound among six {{ill|Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|ja|纒向型前方後円墳|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Makimuku-type keyhole-shaped kofun|qq=}} constructed prior to the Hashihaka Kofun{{sfn|Terasawa|1988}}.}}.
=== Hokuriku === In the late Yayoi period, protruded-corner Kofuns were also constructed in the {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku Region|1=Hokuriku region}}{{sfn|Furukawa|1993}}.
